Introduction Augmented reality (AR) is an emerging technology that supplements reality and allows the user to experience the real world with virtual objects superimposed on or composed with the real world [1]. One of the key advantages of AR is that it is available on most of today’s smartphones and tablet devices, which makes it more available to a wider population of users [2]. Mobile AR has already proven its potential in various application areas, such as retail/shopping, interior design, tourism, navigation, training, education, healthcare, military, video games, and others [3]. As an emerging technology, it enables new forms of human–computer interaction compared to traditional mobile solutions and provides users with engaging experiences, which has a positive impact on users’ motivation to use AR-based solutions. This is especially recognized in the field of game-based learning, as learners nowadays require new and more interesting learning experiences [4]. The concept of games that are not played primarily for amusement, but to impart specific knowledge or skills to the player, is known as “serious games” and was first coined by Abt in 1970 [5]. According to [6], the term “serious games” should be used for games explicitly designed for purposes other than entertainment, i.e., they can be seen as having a specific purpose and not as a synonym for other existing applications. Over the years, serious games have experienced growth, especially in domains of education, training, well-being, advertisement, cultural heritage, interpersonal communication, and healthcare [7]. Serious games can be considered effective educational tools when applied in education properly and in a student-centred way, which is considered one of the key features of the new generation of students [4]. AR-based serious games have also proven their potential to increase student interest and influence motivation and learning efficiency [8,9]. Great interest has also been shown in the field of inclusive education, where research can be found focusing on the design of serious games for a wide range of students with disabilities. However, the development of such solutions is still more focused on a specific difficulty or disability, without applying the principles of Design for All [10]. To benefit all learners, serious games must be developed to meet the needs of a wide range of users, including users with disabilities. This is especially important for AR-based serious games which involve different interactive tasks with virtual content in the real environment, such as those identified in [11]. Intuitive and user-friendly interfaces are also critical for the successful implementation of AR in educational contexts [12]. Thus, AR-based solutions are extremely suited for exploring the best ways of interacting with the user depending on their needs, limitations and context, i.e., to make them more accessible as there are still many accessibility challenges that need to be addressed [13,14]. Accessibility is a measure of the extent to which a product, service, or environment is suitable for all users, including people with disabilities and the elderly. When considering users with disabilities, accessibility can be considered a great part of usability, as it is defined as the “extent to which a system, product or service can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use” [15]. It can generally be achieved by applying the principles of Universal Design (UD), which is a design method that aims to integrate the needs of people with disabilities and the elderly into products intended for widespread use. Besides addressing accessibility needs, UD addresses the needs of all people to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design [16], including people with different ages, sizes, abilities or disabilities. One of the UD principles is the flexibility in use principle that aims to provide users with choices, allowing them to interact with and adapt products or environments according to their unique needs, pace, precision, and control [17]. Nowadays, it is already widely accepted that serious games, integrated as an aid to learning different subjects, play an important role in learning and help students focus on the learning goal [18]. Some of the factors influencing the effect of serious game-assisted learning are the perceived usefulness, ease of use, clarity of the goal, as well as adaptivity to the needs of the user [18]. Additionally, it was shown that serious games with a higher mental load have a negative impact on the learning effect [19]. Since AR enables new ways of interacting, AR-based serious games must be designed in a way that is intuitive and not mentally demanding. In this context, they should not require high physical effort or cause frustration and should be adaptable to the needs of individual users. Because there are users who cannot or do not know how to adapt the content and aspects of the user interface (UI) to meet their needs themselves, it is essential to enable ways of adapting the game without their intervention, i.e., to automatically adapt the game based on their needs. Examples of users who might benefit from automatic adaptation are users who, due to various disabilities, cannot adapt the solution themselves (e.g., people with severe motor disabilities), older people who are not so familiar with new technologies, children who often do not understand how certain settings can be useful for them, as well as users with no prior experience with AR in general. fetched_contents.text: Full article: Location-Based Games for Language Learning: A Scoping Review ABSTRACT Location-based games for language learning is an emerging and innovative domain that has gained momentum over the past twenty years. Such games situate learning in real-world locations, incorporating interactive elements such as collaborative tasks and location-specific prompts, often supported by digital resources like augmented reality. This scoping review maps current research on location-based games for language learning, examining their role in language acquisition, key features of the games and how their effectiveness is assessed. Following PRISMA guidelines, we formulated research questions, identified relevant publications and analysed data from six databases, resulting in 19 included studies. Each study was coded for key characteristics such as data collection methods, intervention types and theoretical frameworks. Our findings show a variety of approaches to implementing location-based games in language learning. While some studies examine their effects on engagement and motivation, others explore language pragmatics and the co-construction of meaning in social interactions. However, inconsistencies in methodological approaches, participant numbers and theoretical underpinnings limit the comparability of findings. We recommend further studies grounded in robust theoretical frameworks across a variety of geographical locations, language learning settings and learner demographics to build on existing work and advance understanding of how location-based games can enhance language learning. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT Introduction The use of games in language learning has shown significant promise, with both digital and non-digital formats enhancing language skills in interactive and engaging ways (Cornillie Citation2022; Pegrum Citation2019; Reinders and Wattana Citation2012; Reinhardt Citation2019). Location-based games stand out due to their ability to provide immersive, contextually rich environments for language practice that align with current theories of second language acquisition (SLA) by emphasising localised, contextual learning and meaningful connections to the real world (Godwin-Jones Citation2016). What distinguishes location-based games from other kinds of game is their appropriation of the local environment as a game board and the extent to which mobile devices are used to facilitate gameplay (de Silva and Sutko Citation2009). Their emergence in the early 2000s was influenced by two key factors: the increased accessibility and affordability of mobile devices in many parts of the world and the US government’s decision to make accurate GPS signal data available to the public in 2000 (Leorke Citation2018). The release of the iPhone 3G in 2008 was another key milestone, particularly in the context of education (Sykes Citation2022). This meant that players no longer needed customised devices to play and could begin to access game content using smartphone applications. As a result, a range of location-based games were created to support learning in subjects such as science, history and geography (e.g., Ardito et al. Citation2012; de Silva and Sutko Citation2009; Klopfer and Squire Citation2007), and free platforms like ARIS and TaleBlazer were developed to enable teachers and game designers to create location-based games without requiring advanced coding skills. Mentira was one of the first games specifically designed for language learning (Holden and Sykes Citation2012). The game centred around a murder-mystery adventure designed for learning Spanish at the University of New Mexico, USA. The ARIS app situated the game’s narrative in Los Griegos, a mainly Spanish-speaking Albuquerque neighbourhood. Players visited physical locations where GPS-triggered quests required them to interact with virtual characters in Spanish using augmented reality (AR). It was intended to facilitate student engagement with the Spanish language and culture in an immersive way, rather than being another tool to help memorise and recite language forms (Holden and Sykes Citation2012). Despite its innovative design, Mentira ultimately became obsolete and unplayable over time (Holden, Sykes, and Thorne Citation2017). However, it paved the way for other projects and sparked interest in exploring the potential of location-based games for language learning. TaleBlazer, also developed in the USA at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), is an open-source AR game editor that allows users to create and play location-based games on iOS and Android devices. Unlike ARIS, which focuses on storytelling, TaleBlazer uses a role-based structure where characters interact within the game world. Regarding language learning, it has been used to create immersive experiences where players take on different roles, engage in contextualised language use and practice communication in authentic settings (Cervi-Wilson and Brick Citation2018). The release of Pokémon GO in the summer of 2016 significantly raised the profile of location-based games, moving them beyond small-scale educational projects into the mainstream. At its peak, Pokémon GO had over 230 million active players, and more than eight years after its launch, it remains a key source of revenue for Niantic, the company behind it (Sensor Tower Citation2024). Pokémon GO also brought AR to the forefront of public attention as a leisure activity and its popularity highlighted the potential of AR in educational contexts, including language learning (Godwin-Jones Citation2016; Sykes Citation2022). While playing a location-based game, language learners use the target language to navigate through a city, engage with local landmarks and interact with virtual characters. fetched_contents.text: JMIR Serious Games * Yuri Gustavo de Sousa Barbalho1,2,*, MSc; * Calliandra Maria de Souza Silva1,*, PhD; * Carla Sílvia Neves da Nora Fernandes2,3,*, PhD; * Raíza Rana de Souza Lima Trombini1,*, MSc; * Patrícia Littig Melo1,*, BSc; * Aline Farias de Oliveira1,*, BSc; * Alayne Larissa Martins Pereira1,*, MSc; * Alessandro de Oliveira Silva4,*, PhD; * Luciano Ramos de Lima5,*, PhD; * Marina Morato Stival1,*, PhD; * Diana Lúcia Moura Pinho1,*, PhD; * Silvana Schwerz Funghetto1,*, PhD 1Faculty of Health Sciences and Technologies, University of Brasília, University Campus - Metropolitan Center, Ceilândia Sul, Brasília, Brazil 2School of Health, Polytechnic Institute of Viana do Castelo, Viana do Castelo, Portugal 3Aditgames – Association for Innovation, Technologies and Games in Health, Porto, Portugal 4Physical Education and Medicine Department, University Center of Brasilia, Brasília, Brazil 5Nursing Department, University of Brasília, Brasilia, Brazil *all authors contributed equally Corresponding Author: Yuri Gustavo de Sousa Barbalho, MSc Abstract Background: Population aging underlines the critical need to improve health professional training to adequately care for adults aged >60 years. Developing educational resources to support academics and professionals presents a valuable opportunity to enhance understanding of health conditions and improve clinical management. Serious games are designed to develop teaching, training, and learning skills. Their use in the educational setting is warranted, as they integrate digital aspects and gamification to create a playful experience for content acquisition. Deepening this theme in nursing education will improve assistance to the older adult population, leading to more qualified care based on gerontological practices and comprehensive health care for older adults. Objective: This study aims to develop and validate a serious game on older adult health for undergraduate nursing students. Methods: This quantitative and descriptive methodological study, conducted between February 2023 and December 2023 at a public university in the Federal District of Brazil, involved the active participation of 27 undergraduate nursing students in their eighth to tenth semesters. The game, Health Unit in Focus (HUF), was developed and validated with their input. It features 75 clinical cases distributed across 3 themes: pharmacology, metabolic syndrome, and semiology. Of the 40 students initially enrolled, 27 completed the study. The app was validated using the System Usability Scale and student feedback, and the results were reported following the Game-Based Intervention Reporting Guidelines (GAMING). Results: The participants had a mean age of 22.67 (SD 1.44) years, were mostly female (20/27, 74%), and were in their eighth semester (26/27, 96%). The game received an average System Usability Scale score of 85.75 (median 86.57), classified as excellent, as all evaluated items scored >75. Participants considered the game easy to use; accessible; practical; and rich in well-founded, useful content. This high usability score, coupled with the overwhelmingly positive feedback from the students, instills confidence in the game’s effectiveness. Furthermore, 100% (27/27) of students agreed that learning through games is effective and expressed interest in incorporating more interactive games into their training. The serious game HUF showed good usability, as its overall score was “excellent,” with its highest score in the odd-numbered items that addressed the positive aspects identified in the analysis. Conclusions: The serious game HUF is not just a valid and reliable tool for training nursing students but also an engaging and interactive approach to learning. Its ability to captivate and involve students in the learning process is a testament to its potential to revolutionize nursing education. It is essential that the development of new methodological resources, such as serious games, be based on scientific evidence to guarantee greater reliability and success in achieving their established objectives. Why simplicity and intuitiveness matter in serious location-based games

Simple mechanics reduce cognitive load and entry barriers because location-based games already place players in unfamiliar physical environments and require them to interact with real-world context, which can be mentally demanding. The evidence shows that serious games are often designed for purposes beyond entertainment, such as education, training, and skill development [N1-R5]. When gameplay is overly complex, it can become harder for players to understand the core loop and start participating effectively. This is especially important in location-based settings, where players must navigate real-world locations and often rely on mobile devices or AR to trigger gameplay [N1-R4], which can itself create friction if the interface is not simple.

Intuitive interfaces improve adoption and retention because they make the game feel familiar and less intimidating. The evidence on serious game accessibility emphasizes that intuitive and user-friendly interfaces are critical for successful implementation in educational contexts [N2-F1]. It also notes that usability is a key factor in the effectiveness of serious games, especially in educational settings where engagement, cognitive retention, and task completion matter [N6-R2]. Intuitive design helps players avoid confusion and frustration, which are major barriers to continued participation. The accessibility framework also highlights that users may need choices and flexibility in how they interact with the game, including automatic adaptation for people who cannot adjust settings themselves [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that an intuitive interface is not just about appearance but about making the game usable for a wide range of players without forcing them to learn complicated controls.

Clarity supports diverse player backgrounds and expectations because serious location-based games often serve multiple purposes and audiences. The evidence on serious games in cultural heritage and education shows that such games can enhance learning and engagement by situating learning in real-world locations and using interactive elements like collaborative tasks and location-specific prompts [N1-R5]. At the same time, the accessibility framework stresses that serious games must be developed to meet the needs of a wide range of users, including those with disabilities and older adults [N2-F1]. This means that clarity in rules, objectives, and navigation helps players with different prior knowledge, skill levels, and expectations to understand the game quickly and begin contributing meaningfully. The review of location-based games for language learning also highlights that such games should foster active learning and learner-centric approaches, supporting deeper communication and group activities [N3-F2]. That aligns with the broader point that intuitive design helps players of all backgrounds to engage with the serious purpose of the game rather than being distracted by unclear mechanics.

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that simplicity and intuitiveness are important because they lower the mental effort needed to start playing, make the game easier to adopt and retain, and help diverse players understand and participate in the serious goal of the experience [N2-F1][N6-R2][N1-R5].

Why onsite support limitations make intuitive design especially important

Onsite support absence forces players to rely on pre-existing knowledge because location-based games often require players to act in real-world environments without a nearby guide or instructor. The evidence on location-based games for language learning explains that such games situate learning in real-world locations and that players use the target language to navigate through a city, engage with local landmarks, and interact with virtual characters [N3-F2]. In that setting, players must understand the game’s objectives, triggers, and mechanics before they can participate meaningfully. When onsite support is not available, players must interpret the game world on their own, which increases the importance of intuitive design.

What happens when players struggle without immediate help is that they are more likely to become frustrated, confused, or abandon the game altogether. The evidence on serious game user experience warns that if not designed and implemented thoughtfully, the user experience can compromise the desired educational or training outcome and render the game pointless [N5-R1]. Poor usability and poor engagement can emerge when the game is too difficult to navigate or when players do not understand what is expected of them. The study comparing usability and engagement between a serious game and a traditional online program also notes that poor-quality studies on dynamics and mechanics can produce unreliable results, which suggests that unclear or poorly designed gameplay can undermine the game’s effectiveness [N5-R3]. In location-based settings, this is especially problematic because players may have limited time to figure things out and may not have someone to ask for help once they are in the field.

Self-guided play can be made safer and more effective through design by reducing ambiguity and providing clear affordances. The accessibility framework argues that intuitive interfaces are critical for successful implementation in educational contexts and that serious games must be adaptable to the needs of individual users [N2-F1]. It also emphasizes that usability is a key factor in effectiveness, with ease of use, clarity of the goal, and adaptivity to the user all influencing learning outcomes [N2-F1][N6-R2]. In a location-based serious game, this means designing triggers, navigation, and feedback in a way that players can follow without confusion. The language-learning example further shows that location-based games can foster active learning and learner-centric approaches, which depends on players being able to engage with the environment and the game mechanics reliably [N3-F2]. Intuitive design therefore helps players stay safe, stay on task, and stay engaged even when onsite support is absent.

In short, intuitive design becomes especially important when onsite support is limited because players must rely on their own understanding of the game and the environment, and unclear gameplay can lead to frustration, confusion, or abandonment [N5-R1][N5-R3][N2-F1].

Without intuitive design and adequate support, that reliability can be lost.

This means that when gameplay is usable, players are more likely to engage with the material, remember it, and complete assigned tasks successfully.

The evidence on serious game usability and engagement warns that if not designed and implemented thoughtfully, the user experience can compromise the desired educational or training outcome and render the game pointless [N5-R1]. It also points to poor-quality studies on dynamics and mechanics that produce unreliable results, which suggests that unclear or inconsistent gameplay can weaken the game’s educational or training value [N5-R3]. In addition, the serious game accessibility framework emphasizes that serious games must be developed to meet the needs of a wide range of users, including people with disabilities and older adults, and that intuitive and user-friendly interfaces are critical for successful implementation [N2-F1]. Poor design in these contexts can therefore reduce the effectiveness of the serious purpose and make the experience less valuable for learners.

Intuitive design can improve long-term player behavior and trust by making the game easier to understand and use consistently. The accessibility framework argues that intuitive interfaces are essential for successful implementation and that usability is a key factor in effectiveness [N2-F1]. It also highlights that serious games should be adaptable to the needs of individual users and that flexibility in use is one of the core principles of Universal Design [N2-F1]. Intuitive design helps reinforce that connection by making the game feel natural and supportive rather than confusing or alien.

In conclusion, gameplay design affects serious game outcomes by influencing learning, engagement, and task completion. Poor design can weaken these outcomes, while intuitive and usable design can strengthen them and support long-term player behavior and trust [N5-R1][N5-R3][N6-R2][N2-F1][N1-R5].

# Why simple and intuitive gameplay is important for serious location-based games

## 1) The core reason: serious games are about learning, training, or skill development, not just play

The fundamental reason simple and intuitive gameplay matters is that serious games are designed for purposes beyond entertainment. The evidence says serious games are “designed to develop teaching, training, and learning skills” and that their use in educational settings is warranted because they integrate digital aspects and gamification to create a playful experience for content acquisition [N5-F3]. That means the game’s purpose is not just to be fun, but to support learning, training, or meaningful engagement with a serious objective. When gameplay is too complex or poorly supported, it can compromise the desired educational or training outcome and render the game pointless [N5-R1]. So simplicity and intuitiveness are not optional luxuries—they are essential to preserving the serious purpose of the experience.

## 2) Simple mechanics reduce cognitive load and entry barriers

Location-based games already place players in unfamiliar physical environments, and that can be mentally demanding. The evidence on serious games in cultural heritage and education notes that such games can enhance learning and engagement by situating learning in real-world locations and using interactive elements like collaborative tasks and location-specific prompts [N1-R5]. But that same real-world context also means players must quickly understand the game’s rules, triggers, and objectives before they can participate meaningfully. Simple mechanics reduce the cognitive load needed to start playing, lowering the barrier to entry. That is especially important in location-based games, where players may be interacting with real-world locations and mobile devices or AR triggers [N1-R4]. The more intuitive the core gameplay loop, the easier it is for players to begin and stay engaged.

## 3) Intuitive interfaces improve adoption and retention

Intuitive interfaces improve adoption and retention because they make the game feel familiar and less intimidating. The evidence on serious game accessibility emphasizes that intuitive and user-friendly interfaces are critical for successful implementation in educational contexts [N2-F1]. It also notes that usability is a key factor in the effectiveness of serious games, especially in educational settings where user engagement, cognitive retention, and task completion matter [N6-R2]. Intuitive design helps players avoid confusion and frustration, which are major barriers to continued participation. The accessibility framework further argues that serious games must be adaptable to the needs of a wide range of users, including those with disabilities and older adults, and that flexibility in use is one of the core principles of Universal Design [N2-F1]. In other words, intuitive design is not just about making the game easier to understand at first—it is about making it usable for a wide range of players over time.

## 4) Clarity supports diverse player backgrounds and expectations

Clarity supports diverse player backgrounds and expectations because serious location-based games often serve multiple purposes and audiences. The evidence shows that location-based games should foster active learning and learner-centric approaches, supporting deeper communication and group activities [N3-F2]. At the same time, the accessibility framework stresses that serious games must be developed to meet the needs of a wide range of users, including people with disabilities and older adults [N2-F1]. That means clarity in rules, objectives, and navigation helps players with different prior knowledge, skill levels, and expectations to understand the game quickly and begin contributing meaningfully. A location-based serious game may be used in education, training, or cultural heritage, and its design must account for players who may have varying levels of technical skill, language ability, and familiarity with location-based play [N1-R5][N3-F2].

## 5) Onsite support limitations make intuitive design especially important

When onsite support is absent, players are forced to rely on pre-existing knowledge. The language-learning example explains that location-based games situate learning in real-world locations and that players use the target language to navigate through a city, engage with local landmarks, and interact with virtual characters [N3-F2]. In such settings, players must understand the game’s objectives, triggers, and mechanics before they can participate meaningfully. Without onsite support, they cannot ask for clarification or guidance when they get stuck. That is why intuitive design becomes especially important: it reduces the need for external help by making the game more self-explanatory.

What happens when players struggle without immediate help is that they are more likely to become frustrated, confused, or abandon the game altogether. The serious game user experience resource warns that if not designed and implemented thoughtfully, the user experience can compromise the desired educational or training outcome and render the game pointless [N5-R1]. Poor usability and poor engagement can emerge when the game is too difficult to navigate or when players do not understand what is expected of them. The evidence also notes that poor-quality studies on dynamics and mechanics can produce unreliable results, which implies that unclear or inconsistent gameplay can undermine the game’s effectiveness [N5-R3]. In location-based contexts, this is especially problematic because players may have limited time to figure things out and may not have someone to ask for help once they are in the field.

Self-guided play can be made safer and more effective through design by reducing ambiguity and providing clear affordances. The accessibility framework argues that intuitive interfaces are essential for successful implementation and that usability is a key factor in effectiveness [N2-F1]. It also emphasizes that serious games should be adaptable to the needs of individual users and that flexibility in use is one of the core principles of Universal Design [N2-F1]. In a location-based serious game, this means designing triggers, navigation, and feedback in a way that players can follow without confusion. The language-learning example further shows that location-based games can foster active learning and learner-centric approaches, which depends on players being able to engage with the environment and the game mechanics reliably [N3-F2]. Intuitive design therefore helps players stay safe, stay on task, and stay engaged even when onsite support is absent.

The evidence shows that poor design can reduce the effectiveness of the serious purpose. The core goal of serious games is not just play but learning, training, or skill development [N5-F3]. When usability is poor, the game can fail to achieve that purpose. The serious game user experience resource warns that if not designed and implemented thoughtfully, the user experience can compromise the desired educational or training outcome and render the game pointless [N5-R1]. This means that overly complex or poorly supported gameplay can undermine the very reason the game exists.

The accessibility framework notes that serious games must be developed to meet the needs of a wide range of users, including people with disabilities and older adults, and that intuitive and user-friendly interfaces are critical for successful implementation [N2-F1]. It also highlights that some users may not know how to adapt the content or interface themselves, and that automatic adaptation is important for those who cannot do so [N2-F1]. The language-learning example reinforces this by showing that location-based games should foster active learning and learner-centric approaches, which requires players to navigate the game world reliably [N3-F2]. Without intuitive design and adequate support, that reliability can be lost.

## 9) Gameplay design affects serious game outcomes in three main ways

Gameplay design affects serious game outcomes by influencing learning, engagement, and task completion. The evidence on serious game usability and engagement states that usability is a critical factor in the effectiveness of serious games, especially in educational contexts where user engagement, cognitive retention, and task completion matter [N6-R2]. It also notes that serious games are designed to develop teaching, training, and learning skills, and that their use in the educational setting is warranted because they integrate digital aspects and gamification to create a playful experience for content acquisition [N5-F3]. The evidence on serious game usability and engagement warns that if not designed and implemented thoughtfully, the user experience can compromise the desired educational or training outcome and render the game pointless [N5-R1]. It also points to poor-quality studies on dynamics and mechanics that produce unreliable results, which suggests that unclear or inconsistent gameplay can weaken the game’s educational or training value [N5-R3]. In addition, the serious game accessibility framework emphasizes that serious games must be developed to meet the needs of a wide range of users, including people with disabilities and older adults, and that intuitive and user-friendly interfaces are critical for successful implementation [N2-F1]. Poor design in these contexts can therefore reduce the effectiveness of the serious purpose and make the experience less valuable for learners.

Intuitive design can improve long-term player behavior and trust by making the game easier to understand and use consistently. The accessibility framework argues that intuitive interfaces are essential for successful implementation and that usability is a key factor in effectiveness [N2-F1]. It also highlights that serious games should be adaptable to the needs of individual users and that flexibility in use is one of the core principles of Universal Design [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that when gameplay is intuitive, players are more likely to use it repeatedly, trust the system, and continue engaging with the serious purpose. The evidence on serious games in cultural heritage and education also shows that such games can enhance learning and engagement by situating learning in real-world locations and using interactive elements like collaborative tasks and location-specific prompts [N1-R5]. Intuitive design helps reinforce that connection by making the game feel natural and supportive rather than confusing or alien.

## 10) Integrated conclusion: why simple intuitive gameplay is important

In short, simple and intuitive gameplay is important for serious location-based games because:

- It lowers cognitive load and entry barriers, making it easier for players to start and stay engaged [N1-R5][N2-F1][N6-R2].
- It improves adoption and retention by reducing confusion and frustration [N2-F1][N6-R2].
- It supports diverse player backgrounds and expectations by making the game easier to understand for people with different skill levels and prior knowledge [N1-R5][N2-F1][N3-F2].
- It becomes especially important when onsite support is absent, because players then have to rely on pre-existing knowledge and cannot easily ask for help [N3-F2][N5-R1].
- It can prevent the game from becoming frustrating or abandoned when players struggle without immediate help [N5-R1][N5-R3].
- It can exclude some players or derail the mission when complexity is too high [N2-F1][N1-R5].
- It can reduce the effectiveness of the serious purpose when design is poor [N5-R1][N5-F3].
- It can improve learning, engagement, and task completion when gameplay is usable [N6-R2][N5-F3].
- It can also support long-term player behavior and trust when the game feels intuitive and reliable [N2-F1][N1-R5].
